workedExamples.stem:
Express
$\dfrac{3}{x-2} - \dfrac{2}{x+1}$
as one fraction in its simplest form.

steps.decision: The two denominators share no factor, so the lowest common denominator is simply their product. Write it once and leave it in brackets for the rest of the question.

options: Because the lowest common denominator uses each distinct factor once
Because the two denominators are always multiplied together
Because the longer denominator is always the common one
whyMenu.explain: Multiplying the two denominators always gives a common denominator, but not the lowest one when they share a factor, and the extra factor has to be cancelled again at the end. Taking each distinct factor once keeps the numerator small enough to handle.

steps.decision: Each numerator is multiplied by what its own denominator is missing: the 3 by $(x+1)$ and the 2 by $(x-2)$. The subtracted product keeps its bracket.

Expanding gives $3x + 3$ and $2x - 4$, and the minus applies to both terms of the second, so the $-4$ becomes $+4$. The numerator that comes out shares no factor with the denominator, so this line is already the simplest form. Leave the denominator in brackets: multiplying it out gains nothing and hides any cancelling.

options: Because the minus sign in front of a bracket changes the sign of every term inside it
Because only the first term of the bracket changes sign
Because a bracket may be removed once the product has been written down
whyMenu.explain: Summer 2025 examiners named this as the single commonest error on the paper's algebraic-fraction question: the product was subtracted and only its first term had its sign changed. Write the bracket, expand inside it, then remove it with every sign flipped.

items.stem: What is the lowest common denominator of $(x+3)(x-3)$ and $(x-3)$?
items.skill: Build the LCD from distinct factors

options.feedback: The second denominator is already one of the first one's factors, so nothing new has to be added.

That is the product of the two denominators. It works, but it leaves a fraction that still cancels, and the numerator becomes a cubic. Summer 2024 examiners reported candidates being unable to work with what this produces.
The denominators were squared rather than combined. Factorise both, then take each distinct factor once.

items.stem: You are subtracting one algebraic fraction from another. What must go round the second numerator?

options.text: A bracket, with the minus sign in front of it
options.feedback: Then when the bracket comes off, every sign inside it changes. It is one extra pair of symbols and it is the difference between full marks and five out of seven.

options.text: Nothing — write the terms straight down after the minus sign
options.feedback: Then the minus reaches only the first term. Summer 2025 examiners named this as the commonest error on the whole question.

options.text: A bracket round the first term only
options.feedback: The whole of the second numerator is being taken away, so the whole of it goes inside the bracket.

items.skill: Apply a minus sign across a whole product

options.feedback: $(x-3)(x+3)$ expands to $x^{2}-9$, and taking all of it away changes all three signs.
Only the first term of the bracket had its sign changed. Summer 2025 examiners printed this exact pattern as the error that stopped most candidates reaching full marks.
The bracket was dropped and the two numerators were added instead of subtracted. Write the minus and the bracket together, before you expand anything.

items.stem: Written as one fraction, what is $\dfrac{2}{x} + \dfrac{3}{x+1}$?
items.skill: Multiply each numerator up to the common denominator

options.feedback: Over $x(x+1)$ the numerators become $2(x+1) + 3x$, which collects to $5x+2$.
The tops were added and the bottoms were added. Fractions are never combined that way: they need a common denominator first.
The common denominator is right and the numerators were never multiplied up to match it. Each numerator is multiplied by whatever its own denominator was missing.

items.stem: In $\dfrac{x}{x^{2}-9} + \dfrac{2}{x-3}$, may you cancel the $(x-3)$ in the first denominator against the $(x-3)$ in the second?
items.skill: Refuse to cancel across an addition

options.text: No — cancelling needs a factor of a numerator and a factor of a denominator
options.feedback: Both of those are denominators, and they belong to different fractions that have not been combined yet. Cancelling only happens inside one fraction.

options.text: Yes, because the same bracket appears twice
options.feedback: Appearing twice is not enough. Summer 2024 examiners described incorrect cancelling before the addition as one of the disappointing features of that question.

options.text: Yes, but only after the numerators have been added
options.feedback: Once the fractions are combined there is one numerator and one denominator, and then you cancel factors of those. The two denominators themselves never cancel each other.

items.stem: You have combined two fractions and collected the numerator. What is the last thing to do?
items.skill: Factorise the numerator and look for a cancel

options.text: Factorise the numerator and see whether anything cancels with the denominator
options.feedback: It is the last mark on nearly every one of these questions, and it is the one Summer 2025 reported as most often missed.

options.text: Nothing — a collected numerator over the common denominator is the answer
options.feedback: Sometimes it is, and you only know by trying to factorise. When the numerator does factorise, one of its brackets is usually the one underneath.

options.text: Multiply the denominator out so the answer is a single quadratic over a single quadratic
options.feedback: Multiplying the denominator out hides the very factor you are looking for. Leave it in brackets.

items.skill: Use the factorised LCD and finish the cancelling

options.feedback: Over $(x-2)(x+2)$ the numerator is $3x-6 = 3(x-2)$, and $(x-2)$ cancels.
Everything up to here is right. The numerator factorises as $3(x-2)$ and one bracket cancels, which is the last mark.
The two denominators were multiplied together instead of the difference of two squares being factorised first. The value is right; the fraction is nowhere near its simplest form.

items.stem: What is the numerator of $\dfrac{x}{x-3} - \dfrac{18}{x^{2}-9}$ once both fractions are over $(x-3)(x+3)$?

options.feedback: $x(x+3) - 18$, which expands and collects to $x^{2}+3x-18$, and that factorises as $(x+6)(x-3)$.
The numerators were subtracted as they stood. The first fraction's denominator is missing $(x+3)$, so its numerator has to be multiplied by it.
The multiplying up is right and the second numerator was added rather than taken away. Write the minus sign and the bracket together before you expand anything.

emphasis: as one fraction in its simplest form

parts.stem:
Express
$\dfrac{2}{x} + \dfrac{3}{x+1}$
as one fraction in its simplest form.
hints: The denominators share no factor.
Multiply the 2 by the second denominator and the 3 by the first.
parts.workedSolution:
The lowest common denominator is $x(x+1)$.
Multiplying each numerator up gives $\frac{2(x+1) + 3x}{x(x+1)}$, which collects to $\frac{5x+2}{x(x+1)}$.
Nothing cancels, so the answer is $\frac{5x+2}{x(x+1)}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The common denominator is right and the numerators were combined as they stood. Each one has to be multiplied by whatever its own denominator was missing — here $2(x+1) + 3x$ — before they are combined.
The numerators were added and the denominators were added. Fractions are only ever combined over a common denominator, so nothing here is credited; start again from the lowest common denominator.

questions.solutionProgram: LCD x(x + 1); numerator 2x + 2 + 3x = 5x + 2 = (5x + 2); answer (5x + 2) over (x(x + 1)); identity checked at three sample points

hints: Put a bracket round the second numerator before you subtract it.

parts.workedSolution:
The lowest common denominator is $(x+2)(x-3)$.
Multiplying each numerator up gives $\frac{4(x-3) - 1(x+2)}{(x+2)(x-3)}$, which collects to $\frac{3x-14}{(x+2)(x-3)}$.
Nothing cancels, so the answer is $\frac{3x-14}{(x+2)(x-3)}$.

scheme.for: lowest common denominator (x - 3)(x + 3), reached by factorising the quadratic denominator first
each numerator multiplied up: x² + 3x and 18, with the subtracted one bracketed

hints: Factorise $x^{2}-9$ first.
The numerator is a quadratic that factorises.
One bracket cancels with the denominator.
parts.workedSolution:
The lowest common denominator is $(x-3)(x+3)$.

findTheMistake.stem: Orla was asked to simplify fully $\dfrac{x}{x+3} - \dfrac{x-3}{x+4}$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: (x - 3)(x + 3) expands to x² - 9, and all of it is being taken away. Only the first term had its sign changed; the rest kept the signs they had inside the bracket.
findTheMistake.feedback: The method-and-working mark for the common denominator and the method mark for multiplying the numerators up are both safe. The working mark that follows needs every sign inside the subtracted bracket changed, and only the first one was, so it is lost and so is the final mark. Summer 2025 examiners printed this pattern as the commonest error on that paper's algebraic-fraction question. Expand inside the bracket on one line, then remove the bracket on the next with every sign flipped.

findTheMistake.stem: Jack was asked to simplify fully $\dfrac{4}{x-3} + \dfrac{6}{x^{2}-9}$. His working:
studentWorking: That does not simplify, so it is the answer.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: x² - 9 is a difference of two squares, (x + 3)(x - 3), and (x - 3) is already one of its factors. The lowest common denominator is therefore (x - 3)(x + 3), not the product of the two printed denominators.
findTheMistake.feedback: A common denominator was found, so a method mark stands, but it is not the lowest one and the mark for the correct lowest common denominator is gone. Factorise every denominator before you choose it: x² - 9 splits into (x + 3)(x - 3) and one of those brackets is already there. Summer 2024 examiners traced cubic expressions candidates could not work with to exactly this choice.

findTheMistake.stem: Niall was asked to simplify fully $\dfrac{x}{x^{2}-9} + \dfrac{2}{x-3}$. His working:
studentWorking: Cancel the (x - 3) in the first denominator with the (x - 3) in the second
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Both of those brackets are denominators, and they belong to two fractions that have not been combined yet. Cancelling only ever removes a factor of one numerator against a factor of the same fraction's denominator.
findTheMistake.feedback: The factorising in line 1 earns its method-and-working mark. Line 2 removes a bracket from the first fraction's denominator without dividing that fraction's numerator, so the expression is no longer the one in the question and nothing after it can be credited. The numerator that came out happens to be right, which is exactly why this slip is hard to catch — the denominator is short by a bracket. Summer 2024 examiners called out incorrect cancelling before the addition as a disappointing feature of that paper.

prompts.prompt: The five moves for adding or subtracting algebraic fractions.
prompts.answer: 1 Factorise every denominator. 2 Build the lowest common denominator from the distinct factors, each used once. 3 Multiply each numerator by what its own denominator was missing, bracketing a subtracted one. 4 Expand, change every sign inside a subtracted bracket, and collect. 5 Factorise the numerator and cancel.

prompts.prompt: Why must a subtracted numerator be written inside brackets?
prompts.answer: Because the minus sign applies to every term of it. Without the bracket only the first term changes sign, and Summer 2025 examiners named that as the commonest error on the whole question.

prompts.prompt: The denominators are $x^{2}-9$ and $x-3$. What is the lowest common denominator, and what is it not?
prompts.answer: It is $(x+3)(x-3)$. It is not $(x-3)(x^{2}-9)$: that is a common denominator, but it leaves a cubic numerator and a fraction that still cancels.

prompts.prompt: May you cancel a bracket that appears in both denominators before you add?
prompts.answer: No. Cancelling removes a factor from a numerator and the same factor from that fraction's own denominator. Two denominators never cancel each other, and Summer 2024 examiners reported this as an error made before the addition.

prompts.prompt: You have collected the numerator over the lowest common denominator. What are the last two things you do?
prompts.answer: Factorise the numerator, then check every one of its factors against the denominator and cancel anything that matches. Stopping before that is the last-mark loss reported in Summer 2025.

prompts.prompt: Your answer to a 'simplify fully' question comes out as a plain number. Is that a mistake?
prompts.answer: No. When every bracket pairs off, a number is the answer, and Summer 2025's question ended exactly that way. The reported error was stopping just before it and leaving the factorised fraction.

prompts.prompt: What does 'as one fraction in its simplest form' demand?
prompts.answer: One fraction bar, with the numerator collected and factorised and nothing left that divides both lines. The denominator is left as brackets, not multiplied out.

prompts.prompt: What is the quickest check that a combined fraction is right?
prompts.answer: Substitute a value of $x$ that makes no denominator zero into both the original expression and your answer. If they disagree, a sign or a numerator has gone astray.
$\frac{3}{x+2}$ — the lowest common denominator is $(x-2)(x+2)$, the numerator is $3x-6 = 3(x-2)$, and $(x-2)$ cancels.

findings.asked: Combine algebraic fractions with quadratic denominators, then use the result.
findings.wentWrong: Many did not factorise the quadratics first and ended up with cubic numerators and denominators; incorrect cancelling appeared inside the addition; a follow-through mark was available for cross-multiplying.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Factorised every quadratic, identified the lowest common denominator, combined, and cancelled only at the end.

findings.asked: Expand a product, then substitute it into a numerator and simplify a fraction.
findings.wentWrong: Gathering the terms in the numerator went wrong, and those with the right numerator often divided by 3 before factorising, producing a wrong final form.
findings.rule: Factorise the numerator before dividing anything out.

findings.asked: Simplify a fraction, then add two algebraic fractions.
findings.wentWrong: In the addition, x squared - 9 was seen as a difference of two squares but (x + 3)(x - 3) was not used as the common denominator, so cubics appeared; some cancelled terms before adding; the simplification missed a factor of 2.
findings.rule: After a difference of two squares the LCD is the pair of brackets, not the product of the denominators.

findings.asked: Combine and simplify two algebraic fractions to a constant.
findings.wentWrong: Most reached 5 of 7 marks; the killer error was subtracting a bracketed product and changing only its first term's sign; brackets dropped; premature cancelling; stopping before the final value.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the subtracted product in brackets, expanded it in full, applied the minus to every term, collected, factorised and cancelled to the final value.
findings.rule: Minus a bracket: every term changes sign.

insight.ruleToRemember: Factorise every numerator and denominator; the LCD is the product of the distinct factors; keep subtracted numerators in brackets and distribute the sign; cancel only whole factors, and simplify to the end.
insight.aStarSignal: An addition where the LCD comes from a difference of two squares and the numerator must be subtracted with a sign change on every term, finishing as a single simplified expression.
